title: Israeli strikes in Gaza kill eight including child, hospitals say
description: Israeli strikes in Gaza have killed at least eight people, including a child, according to hospitals, despite a year-old ceasefire.In Gaza City to the
body: Israeli strikes in Gaza have killed at least eight people, including a child, according to hospitals, despite a year-old ceasefire.In Gaza City to the north, hospital officials said a missile attack hit a group of civilians next to Cairo School in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood, killing three people, including a four-year-old boy.In the southern city of Khan Younis, the Hamas-run ministry of interior said a drone attack targeted a group of police officers in the Al-Mawasi area, killing five, as they were carrying out their routine duties.The Israeli military said it had carried out two attacks on what it described as military operatives but has not yet provided evidence or further information.Outside Gaza City's Shifa Hospital, video showed a crowd of men gathered to pray next to two body bags and the tiny body of the child, which was wrapped in a white towel."My son and his child were martyred. They were sitting in their tent, bothering no one, and nothing else was happening in the area when suddenly, a missile struck them, and they were martyred," Ali Oweis told AFP news agency. "There is no ceasefire; the war is ongoing, don't you see?"At Nasser hospital in Khan Younis, women despaired as body bags lay on the floor, video showed. The interior ministry named the five police officers killed, who were between the ages of 23 and 53, and called the attack a "horrific massacre".A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day.Since then, 1,580 people have been killed, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it is targeting Hamas, but often civilians are also killed.Meanwhile, a peace plan for Gaza, brokered by the Trump administration, has stalled.The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war.The conflict was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.Since the war began, 74,594 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry.Additional reporting by Jacob Phillips

schema.headline: Israeli strikes in Gaza kill eight including child, hospitals say

title: A&E warning system to flag dangerously ill children
description: A&E warning system to flag sick children deteriorating quicklyImage source, Getty ImagesByMichelle RobertsDigital health editorA new early warning sys
body: A&E warning system to flag sick children deteriorating quicklyImage source, Getty ImagesByMichelle RobertsDigital health editorA new early warning system is being introduced in hospital emergency departments in England to help busy NHS staff identify sick children who are dangerously deteriorating.It comes after Health Secretary Yvette Cooper promised to stop "corridor care"  for sick children because of long waits for hospital beds.The new National Paediatric Early Warning System (PEWS) asks staff to check, log and grade vital signs, such as blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen levels. A high overall score means a child needs more urgent attention. Concerns from staff, parents, carers or the child themselves will trigger an immediate escalation of care.Early warnings to save livesImage caption, Two-year-old Finlay Roberts died after spending hours in a crowded hospital corridorThe initiative is designed to save lives ahead of winter, when pressure on the NHS is at its highest.On the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Cooper recently talked about the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts, who died in 2024 after spending hours in a hospital corridor before being discharged.Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor."Whittington Health NHS Trust, where Finlay waited for treatment, extended its condolences to the family and said it continued to experience periods of exceptional demand across emergency care and, at times, some patients may receive care in temporary clinical areas, including corridors.Every moment mattersA similar "early warning" system to identify acutely ill adults, including those with sepsis, is already in use in emergency and general NHS hospital wards.More than 90 hospitals across England have been using the alert system in children's wards, with different age-appropriate assessments available for babies through to teenagers.The NHS has already said it will expand Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England. The rule gives patients, families and carers the right to request a rapid review if they are worried that a patient's condition is getting worse and their concerns are not being responded to.The initiative is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 in 2021 after developing blood poisoning, or sepsis, in hospital following a bike accident. A coroner ruled that her family's concerns about her worsening condition were not listened to and she would probably have survived had she been moved to intensive care earlier. Martha's parents Merope and Paul came up with the idea of the rule in a bid to change the culture that contributed to her death.A&E units will have a dedicated phone number that can be called to trigger an urgent review of a patient's care.Image source, PA MEDIAImage caption, Martha Mills died aged 13 at King's College Hospital in London in 2021Duncan Burton, chief nursing officer for England, said the new early warning system for children in emergency departments was an "important next step in improving care for children and young people across England for this winter - and beyond".He added: "In fast-paced emergency departments, staff need to spot quickly when a child's condition is deteriorating."This standardised approach will help them recognise the warning signs, communicate concerns, and make timely decisions when every moment matters."The early warning system for children, PEWS, is a collaboration between NHS England and the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health and the Royal College of Nursing.

schema.headline: A&E warning system to flag dangerously ill children

title: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire ends
description: A rare humanitarian ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region that allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has ended
body: A rare humanitarian ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region that allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has ended.The localised ceasefire was due to end at 22:59 Ukrainian time (21:00 GMT) on Sunday. While the truce had held since it was implemented last week, fighting had continued elsewhere.On Sunday evening, Ukraine's air alert system was apparently hacked, the country's air force said, warning of radiation over Kyiv - a reference to a possible nuclear attack. The Air Force message read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had struck energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday, leaving hundreds of thousands of homes without power. Some connections were restored on Sunday.Another overnight strike killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Vinnytsia region, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine said.Meanwhile, Ukraine hit a major missile fuel producer in Russia's Rostov region, which caused a fire and damaged four production facilities, Zelensky said.In Ukraine, repair works to restore power continued throughout the day. Most customers in the Dnipropetrovsk region had their connections restored by early evening, but more than 60,000 were still without power, the governor said.Because of regular attacks on energy infrastructure, emergency power cuts have been introduced across the country. Even in the capital Kyiv, electricity is cut off for most of the day, and water supplies are also disrupted.Zelensky said in a social media post that the intensity of Russian strikes has been "extremely high" over the past week, adding that Russia was "trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors". He added that "every day" Ukraine communicated its need for Patriot missiles - the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles - to the US, Europe and other partners. He thanked countries for their support so far and longer-term commitments, but called again for more immediate aid.

schema.headline: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire ends

title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
description: Image source, Lisa ClewesImage caption, Airbnb host Lisa says her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests ByYasmin RufoWhen
body: Image source, Lisa ClewesImage caption, Airbnb host Lisa says her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests ByYasmin RufoWhen Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess.Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage.But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden."It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes.She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher.Image source, Lisa ClewesImage caption, Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her property and fears that guests leaving more mess could mean increasing costsBut Airbnb's new rules mean hosts can no longer ask guests to do jobs normally carried out by cleaners, including washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds and taking rubbish off site.The updated guidelines, which apply to bookings made globally from 20 November, state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests.Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She fears guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her guests.Image source, AirbnbImage caption, The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees. She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee. Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins."We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all."While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal."It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect."Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides".Image source, Krissi FoskettImage caption, Krissi says there's a difference between being a respectful guest and being expected to help run the business you've just paid to stay inDuring a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area."I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says.For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests".Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine.While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says. "If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business."Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two.His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it".Image source, Anthony MarshImage caption, Anthony and his husband used to list five of their 12 cabins in North Yorkshire on Airbnb...Image source, Gasp image coImage caption, ... but will now list just two in light of the new rules He believes asking guests to wash their pots and put out the bins is hardly unreasonable and, with a small cleaning team and tight turnaround times, he worries extra mess could leave properties unready for the next arrivals."It's common sense and common decency," he says.His company does not charge a cleaning fee, and Marsh says most guests are respectful. But fees are more common than not. Some 63.2% of Airbnb listings charge a cleaning fee, with an average cost of £55 according to data from AirROI, external.Laura Lewis runs a directory that helps holiday-let owners market their properties and connect with potential guests.Many of her clients also list on Airbnb and she says most are unhappy with the new rules, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect."Some people say it's factored into the cleaning fee, but I wouldn't leave a holiday let with all the washing-up to do. It's not the right thing," she says.Image source, Laura LewisImage caption, Laura Lewis says it's a matter of "basic respect" to wash dishes and take the bins outThe announcement has added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year. Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.Lewis has taken the same approach with the three treehouses on her farm – most of her bookings are already direct and she now plans to remove her listings from Airbnb altogether.Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however. Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, believes the update will improve the guest experience without changing how most people behave.Guests at his property in south-west London are asked only to lock up and return the keys. "People sometimes strip the beds or do things without me asking, and that's nice for my cleaners, but I don't expect it."Porsz doubts the changes will lead to guests leaving properties in a worse state, pointing to Airbnb's mutual review system."If I put a big chore list, I wouldn't expect a five-star review and vice versa – if a guest leaves the place in a state, you're not going to give them a good review."He believes the system encourages both sides to behave reasonably, and that most guests will continue to treat properties with respect."Airbnb is trying to cut out the silly stuff because it's not a good guest experience."Update 1 November - this article has been updated to remove a photograph of a contributor after they confirmed AI had been used in the image.

schema.headline: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests

title: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
description: King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade, during the final le
body: King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade, during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech which will touch on the issue.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.In an address to the nation to mark Antigua and Barbuda's independence day, Prime Minister Gaston Browne said the history of slavery was painful and "its consequences have not disappeared with the passage of time".He said the country's pursuit of reparatory justice deserved "seriousness, sensitivity and sustained international engagement".Browne went on to say his government was having these conversations in bilateral discussions with the UK and other Commonwealth countries at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM). Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving current problems.She told BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "The transatlantic slave trade happened centuries ago. It is time for the Commonwealth to start looking forwards, not endlessly backwards."The King will make his speech at the CHOGM.He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said."You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow, and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to "the UK government's position".The Caribbean tour has again thrust King Charles into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech where he spoke of the "suffering of the past".In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion where hundreds of enslaved people were killed. Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology are a matter for government, not the Palace."His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to 'bat for Britain', the Realms and wider Commonwealth."In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation", external, and that Britain "must face up to the past".His separate pledge in his article to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by King Charles, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change.The King will be giving the opening speech at CHOGM, which gathers leaders from those 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth.Each biennial meeting has a theme and this year's is officially called Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth. Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua and, as the couple attended a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island, there was a reminder of what the intended focus of the week will be.Bishop of North Eastern Caribbean and Aruba,  Ernest Flemming, told the congregation the "prosperity" of the Commonwealth must be a "shared prosperity"."True partnership requires mutual respect, it requires listening, it requires fairness."A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: "Institutions are under strain across the globe. The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".Later ion Sunday, the King was left drenched and without an umbrella when a torrential downpour interrupted an Independence Day ceremony. Queen Camilla was swiftly given an umbrella when the rain started, while the King was seen gesturing to be given one of his own.

schema.headline: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology

title: Kimi Antonelli becomes F1 world champion as Max Verstappen wins Mexico City Grand Prix
description: Kimi Antonelli clinched his first world title and became the youngest champion in Formula 1 history by finishing third at the Mexico City Grand Prix.A
body: Kimi Antonelli clinched his first world title and became the youngest champion in Formula 1 history by finishing third at the Mexico City Grand Prix.Antonelli - 20 years and 68 days old - finished the race in third, behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.His moment of glory came on a day when tensions at Ferrari between seven-time champion Hamilton and team-mate Charles Leclerc came close to boiling over.Antonelli drove a composed race amid some hectic action involving the other front-runners in a grand prix interrupted by a red flag that led to a 25-lap sprint to the finish.The Italian, a teenager until late August, spent the closing laps watching Hamilton try to get close enough to pass Verstappen after the two had made contact at the first chicane at the restart.But Hamilton found it impossible to get his Ferrari close enough to Verstappen to try to pass and ended the day frustrated and feeling a win had slipped through his fingers as a consequence of Leclerc's aggression on the first lap.That was a secondary story on the day Antonelli made history, smashing Sebastian Vettel's previous record for being the youngest champion by three years and 66 days.Antonelli also becomes the first Italian to win the F1 title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.Antonelli had tears mixed with laughter over the radio on the slowing down lap as he proved initially incapable of talking when his team told him he was world champion.After he half-composed himself, he said: "Thank you so much. We did it. We did it."The key stories of the race were:Antonelli delivering the title with several races to go in a season he has taken by stormTension at Ferrari after Leclerc's successful attempts to grab the lead on the first lap led to controversy and unhappiness at the teamVerstappen benefiting from the internal battle to take his third win in four races.Antonelli went into the race knowing that effectively he only had to stay out of trouble to ensure he secured the title.The only way he could not do so was if George Russell or Hamilton won the race. Even then, he needed only to finish ninth if it was his team-mate or 10th if it was Hamilton.Antonelli ran a steady fourth in the first stint, behind Leclerc, Verstappen and Hamilton, moving into the lead as others made their pit stops in front of him, and then pitted for fresh tyres just a lap before the safety car which was why Mercedes had elongated his final stint.A lap later, Valtteri Bottas' Cadillac crashed on lap 45 when its front suspension failed under braking for Turn One, leading initially to a safety car and then the race being stopped when it became clear how long it was going to take to repair the barriers.At the restart, Leclerc locked his left front wheel heavily as Verstappen and Hamilton battled for the lead in front of him, and Antonelli passed him at the start of the next lap.There was another safety car with 12 laps to go when Arvid Lindblad crashed his Racing Bulls after a collision with McLaren's Oscar Piastri.When the race restarted with seven laps to go, Antonelli ran at the back of a three-car train with Verstappen and Hamilton, none of the three able to make any moves.They crossed the line nose to tail, less than two seconds covering all three cars.The incident that is likely to lead to an inquest at Ferrari came on the first lap.Hamilton started on pole, with Leclerc third behind Russell, but as the Mercedes dropped back Leclerc challenged Hamilton through Turns One, Two and Three.Hamilton held him off, but at the Turn Four/Five chicane Leclerc dived around the outside before taking to the grass, cut the corner and emerged in the lead.Hamilton had also gone off defending, although by nowhere near as much as Leclerc, and that gave Verstappen the chance to nip by Hamilton into Turn Six and into second place.Verstappen and Hamilton both got on the radio to say Leclerc had to give the position back, but he stayed in the lead and was given a five-second penalty.The standard punishment is 10 seconds, but the stewards took into account as mitigation that Hamilton had also gone off so neither car was in a position to make the corner.Hamilton's argument will be that Leclerc cost him and the team a victory - had they worked together on the first lap, they could have ended it one-two and would probably have run that way to the end given the difficulty of overtaking.Later in the race, Leclerc's lock-up after the red flag left him battling a flat spot on his tyre, and he was pressured heavily by McLaren's Lando Norris.But despite expressing concerns about his tyre making it, he managed to hold on ahead of the 2025 world champion.Russell took a low-key sixth, including a 10-second penalty for tipping Red Bull's Isack Hadjar into a spin on the first lap, ahead of Piastri, his car damaged in the incident with Lindblad.

schema.headline: Kimi Antonelli becomes F1 world champion as Max Verstappen wins Mexico City Grand Prix

title: John Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers
description: The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentiall
body: The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentially breaking a Labour manifesto promise. In 2024, Labour said it would remove "discriminatory age bands", vowing to end the gap between the adult minimum wage and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.But in last week's Budget, Healey said that younger workers would see the same increase as older workers, leaving a gap between the two rates this year.  Pay for 18 to 20-year-olds in 2026 will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour. In a BBC interview broadcast on Sunday, Healey was asked if younger workers would be paid the same as older workers, when it comes to the minimum wage, by the time of the next election?"We'll take one step at a time," he said, suggesting that Labour might abandon its plan to close the gap before the next election. It is a change that is likely to anger the unions and some on the left of the party.Healey added that Labour was still committed to the ambition, but hinted the plan to equalise wages might be delayed, partly to encourage businesses to employ younger workers. "There is no question about whether or if, it's a question of when - it's a question of how fast," he said. "I want to make sure we can look hard at those trade-offs that are there between jobs and wages.""I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation. A million youngsters - written off without any prospect of being helped into work and making contributions to this country for the future."The chancellor also suggested that he is willing to make potentially big cuts to some areas of public spending, to get the country's debt falling. The budget documents spell out real-terms reductions to some government departments in the years to come. The likelihood of the government following through was questioned by the respected independent number cruncher, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) this week. But asked if he would make big cuts, Healey said: "We've already demonstrated we are prepared to take hard decisions about the priorities in government."Pressed on whether he would make cuts of more than 2% a year to some government departments, he added: "We will carry that through to the 10-year plan and the spending review next year.""But in the budget I also set out the ways that we're preparing and the work we've got under way to prepare for those spending review decisions."Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the "bulk" of spending cuts should be from the welfare budget, describing it as containing "astronomical sums".She also proposed reducing the size of the civil service and reducing budgets in departments such as the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.On whether she would support cuts pencilled in by the government, Badenoch told the same programme: "What exactly are they cutting? I'm not against what they're doing but there's no detail."Badenoch said she did not want to see cuts in frontline services but said there was a need to "bring down the cost of government".Reflecting on the Budget, she said: "The chancellor had 98 different measures, a lot of them very piecemeal, none will make a difference."So living within our means, absolutely, we've got to do that. That will require cuts to government, but we are setting out the things very clearly that we're going to change, the bulk of which is in welfare. Other departments will have changes too."

schema.headline: John Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers

title: Kimi Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' and made on the track
description: This is an updated version of an article first published in August 2026Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on h
body: This is an updated version of an article first published in August 2026Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"Of course he did.Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest."I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m."We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit."The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went."I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career."Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened."I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news"."'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision."We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin."We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed."It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later."If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar."With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit."The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition."Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica."No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season."I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes."We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points."Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good"."Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice."This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change"."The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift."Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin."There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone."We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him."There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality."In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says."We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive."It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family"."They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer."We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general."About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son."In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan."Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says."The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

schema.headline: Kimi Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' and made on the track

title: Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari need to have 'serious talks' after Charles Leclerc
description: Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari "have to have some serious talks behind closed doors" after fighting between their two drivers cost them victory in the Me
body: Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari "have to have some serious talks behind closed doors" after fighting between their two drivers cost them victory in the Mexico City Grand Prix.Leclerc cut a chicane on the first lap to take the lead from Hamilton, who then lost second place to Max Verstappen as a consequence of his team-mate's attack.Verstappen went on to win the race with Hamilton second, as Kimi Antonelli finished third to become the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history."Ultimately, that lost us the win today," said Hamilton. "We have to have some serious talks behind closed doors."During a red-flag period in the race caused by a crash for Valtteri Bottas' Cadillac, Hamilton had said over team radio: "We've got big problems. Big, big problems."When informed Hamilton was unhappy, Leclerc said: "I will speak with Lewis. We both didn't make the corner. I don't know if Lewis' point was for me to get P3 but having the Red Bull second I felt it was worth it to keep the position and see what happened. That's what I did."I could be also unhappy with how much he pushed me off track out of Turn One, but it is racing. When you are fighting for a win it is the way it should be."Hamilton's point is that if the Ferraris had worked together on the first lap, they would have been running one-two and could have controlled the race from there and likely finished in those positions.He said: "We could have easily had a one-two today. We had the pace to do so."We're going into Turn Four first and second. If we just held position, I think anything can happen in the race. But when your team-mate works against you and then you lose positions like that, it's definitely tough."So we'll just talk about it offline and it's not really worth saying too much more. We don't have rules of engagement. And whether or not that would change anything from Charles' side, I don't know. We've just got to figure out. But something needs to change for sure."Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur said he was "frustrated" at the way the incident played out."It's a lot of frustration for me but I'm not the most important," he said. "It's a lot of frustration for the 2,000 people working for the project. And this I will need time to digest."The Frenchman added: "We'll discuss tonight, we'll fix it tomorrow and then we'll be focused on the cycle."Hamilton added: "Fred's doing his best. Fred came and spoke to me before the race and I think he was nervous and I think he just wanted us, of course, he wants these two drivers to do well."From my side, if I'm coming from behind and I'm taking all the risk and it ends up we lose as a team, then I think I'd have some answering to do, because it impacts a lot of people."But the other way around, I'm in the lead and it was just unnecessary."The core thing to remember, which maybe that comes with age, but every decision you make in the car impacts all the people that work in the background for the whole team."So working as a team, part of our job and part of our contract is we have to work as a team, which we could have easily done today. So it's a shame to see us lose as we did. It will continue unless action is taken."On Leclerc, Hamilton said: "The guy's 28 years old, so I don't think it's an age thing. I think it's a mentality thing. It's like do or die, either I win or none of us do, and it shouldn't be that."The incident was the latest and arguably most serious of a series of tensions between Hamilton and Leclerc this season.It follows Leclerc pushing Hamilton off track at the first corner of the Italian Grand Prix.The race before that, Leclerc ignored a team order to let Hamilton by when they were on different strategies.In Singapore last month, there was another incident when Hamilton felt he should have been let by when they were on different tyres, but Ferrari refused to make the call.Verstappen, who capitalised on this latest battle in Mexico, said: "Ferrari were really fast, I do think they made it a little bit difficult for themselves fighting each other and that's why I was able to capitalise on that. I mean, I take it, right?"

schema.headline: Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari need to have 'serious talks' after Charles Leclerc

title: New Buy Now Pay Later rules - don't get caught out
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentIf you've bought something via Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) since the summer, then you'll have bee
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentIf you've bought something via Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) since the summer, then you'll have been tested to see if you can afford it.BNPL has always been a type of loan, usually paid back in instalments, but it's only been officially regulated since July.This means stricter background checks on your ability to repay. If you fail, then your purchase via BNPL will be blocked. If there's a chance of this happening to you, here are some ways to approach the situation.What are the new rules?BNPL lenders - such as Klarna, Clearpay and others - must now have regulator approval to operate, giving shoppers more access to refunds and independent rulings on complaints if things go wrong.But new affordability checks on each BNPL transaction could also leave you blocked from services for the first time.There are different affordability checks for different purchases, partially based on how much is borrowed.But, with the expensive festive season approaching, here's how to avoid being blocked when time and finances are tight. How do I avoid being blocked?Here are four things to consider if you find your account is closed or your borrowing limit has been massively reduced, from Sara Williams, a former volunteer debt adviser at Citizens Advice who posts tips as Debt Camel on social media.Slow down your purchases: is what you are buying essential or can you postpone it?Be more careful about what you buy to avoid needing a high credit limit to, for example, buy lots of clothes in different sizesCancel subscriptions to escape the trap of having to use BNPL to make up for the cost of previous paymentsTalk to debt charities for help and access to food bank vouchers if you are using BNPL for essentialsAvoid getting into debtIf you are struggling to make repayments on any type of loan - BNPL or otherwise - you should seek help before things spiral out of control.The government-backed, independent, MoneyHelper website, external has a guide to finding free debt advice near you, external.It also suggests writing down exactly what you owe, to help plan how you will repay the money.There are also tools to work out if you are receiving all the benefits and grants you are entitled to, and a bill prioritiser, external to show which payments to make first and what to do if you miss a payment.You should also be sceptical of supposed debt solutions you might see on your social feeds.

schema.headline: New Buy Now Pay Later rules - don't get caught out

title: Cate McHugh wins The Voice UK after being mentored by Sir Tom Jones
description: A singer who began her career as a teenager busking on the streets of Cardiff has been crowned winner of The Voice UK.Cate McHugh, from Llantwit Major
body: A singer who began her career as a teenager busking on the streets of Cardiff has been crowned winner of The Voice UK.Cate McHugh, from Llantwit Major in the Vale of Glamorgan, appeared stunned when she heard her name announced on the ITV show, telling viewers "I did it" when asked how she was feeling.The performer, who has a degenerative sight condition which has left her registered blind, was given a congratulatory hug by her coach Sir Tom Jones on his final appearance on the show after previously announcing he had been "fired". Speaking after the show, McHugh, 31, said: "I won The Voice! I'm entirely gobsmacked and absolutely haven't fully processed this information just yet."Footage shared by McHugh on social media showed her laughing and smiling with family and friends screaming in delight as they celebrated her victory at a watch party in Cardiff.McHugh's prizes include a £50,000 cash prize and a recording contract, with her first ever single, a cover of The Beatles classic Blackbird, now released.Posting on social media, she said: "From the bottom of my heart I want to say THANK YOU for following my journey, and joining my world! This is where it's going to REALLY get fun!"

schema.headline: Cate McHugh wins The Voice UK after being mentored by Sir Tom Jones

title: Binance hack: Users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto heist
description: Binance customers withdrew $3.64bn (£2.72bn) of assets from the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following a record ha
body: Binance customers withdrew $3.64bn (£2.72bn) of assets from the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following a record hack last week.The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack, which is said to be the largest hack in history.The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach, but that the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack."Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion," Binance posted on X.There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.34bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack.Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.

schema.headline: Binance hack: Users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto heist

title: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Republican in Michigan Senate race
description: A Democrat in Michigan has endorsed the Republican candidate in the state's crucial US Senate contest, as a spat with her own party's candidate Abdul
body: A Democrat in Michigan has endorsed the Republican candidate in the state's crucial US Senate contest, as a spat with her own party's candidate Abdul El-Sayed escalated just days before the vote.Haley Stevens, a sitting congresswoman who lost out on the Democratic Senate nomination to El-Sayed, made a surprise appearance alongside the Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday."I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted to X shortly after that appearance. "Who we are as Michiganders is not hate and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now.""That's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers," Stevens said.The move stunned many of Stevens' fellow Democrats who condemned her decision to break from the party and switch her support just two days before the election, with one calling it a "despicable betrayal". The public feud between Stevens, a centrist Democrat, and El-Sayed, who represents the party's left-wing, has boiled over in recent days. Stevens called on El-Sayed to denounce a campaign advert from an outside liberal group that linked US support for Israel with high prices. El-Sayed criticised the advert and said he had nothing to do with its contents.Stevens had been scheduled to appear at an event with El-Sayed on Sunday in an effort to display party unity, but he reportedly asked her not to come and she chose to attend a church service with his Republican opponent instead."This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there, that he didn't want me there," Stevens told reporters as she stood alongside Rogers outside the church.When asked about Stevens' endorsement, El-Sayed told reporters he was focused on the problems Michiganders are facing."At the end of the day, I don't think about Haley Stevens," he said on Sunday. "None of this matters."In downtown Detroit, several Democrats the BBC spoke to said they were disappointed by Stevens' endorsement of Rogers."I just genuinely don't understand it," said Summer Lawrence, a 21-year-old student. "I do think it's a betrayal of the party because the things she stands for are not the same things that he stands for as a Republican.""Maybe she had frustrations with the party," Matthew Barera, another Michigan voter, said.Others, including Republicans who support Rogers, said they doubted it would make a difference to the race."People can see right through her actions, you know? She's just angry," Marissa Lee, a Rogers supporter, told the BBC. "She is not going to make anybody change their mind."Over the weekend, as Stevens' criticism of El-Sayed escalated, a number of Democratic politicians in Michigan publicly encouraged her to end the feud and back the party's candidates more directly.The primary, and the conflict between the pair, has underlined divisions over the party's direction ahead of the 2028 presidential election.Former public health official El-Sayed, who is the son of Egyptian immigrants, has channelled grassroots frustration with Washington politics as well as US ties to Israel.Stevens is a more centrist Democrat - and had the support of party figures such as Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer during the primary race. The party is hoping to regain control of the Senate in Tuesday's elections, but will need a net gain of four seats to do so. A loss in Michigan - which they currently hold - would represent a major blow and leave them needing to flip five seats.

schema.headline: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Republican in Michigan Senate race

title: Democrats have high hopes for midterms, but polls have let them down before
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentThe Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentThe Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.A historically unpopular Republican president, an American public unhappy with the rising costs of food and bills, and months of favourable polls point to a good night for them on Tuesday.Democratic candidates lead in well over the 218 seats needed to flip control of the lower chamber of Congress, the House of Representatives, the polls suggest. And they are tied or narrowly ahead in the key Senate races.A recent New York Times poll had the Senate race in South Carolina, a state Donald Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024, as a tie. Recent CNN surveys put the Democrats ahead in Texas, Kansas and Maine.But are the polls accurate?Recent US political history is littered with examples where public opinion polls, even ones just days before an election, were off the mark. Trump outperformed predictions on his way to White House victories in 2016 and 2024. His narrow defeat in 2020 came after most surveys indicated a more comfortable win for Democrat Joe Biden.Earlier this year, polls suggested Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was poised for a double-digit win in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Instead it was 1%. In Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, the candidate that had a polling lead that approached 20 points lost by a fraction of a percent.According to Clifford Young, president of Ipsos Public Affairs, which conducts political and market research surveys, polling has become difficult in recent years because it's harder to reach Americans as they abandon their land lines and screen their calls. And many of those who pollsters do contact have become less willing to participate."Conservatives, especially those on the far right, are much more anti-establishment by nature," Young says. "And they don't participate in anything. They hate the system. That's the challenge."If Republican voters are being undercounted in a systematic way, and polling companies don't take that into consideration when constructing their voting models, it could skew their data towards the Democrats.That's one of the reasons why it has become trickier for pollsters to predict what the electorate will look like.Figure caption, What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?In recent years, midterm general election polls have proven to be more accurate, in part because Trump - and his unique ability to draw disaffected Americans to the polls - was not on the ballot.In 2022, they suggested Democrats would defy conventional expectations and avoid an electoral wipe-out despite Biden's low approval numbers.While the party lost control of the House of Representatives, the margins were slim and Democrats maintained control of the US Senate.While this year's primary results did provide bigger surprises, Young says that nominating contests have historically been volatile, with voters more likely to make up their minds at the last minute. It shouldn't be seen as an indication that the current crop of general election polls are off the mark.It's common for the party of the president to have a bad night in the midterms.One of the most notable examples in recent years came in 2010 when Republicans flipped more than 60 House seats and made gains in the Senate. It came off the back of an economy struggling to recover from the financial crash and conservative fears over President Barack Obama's healthcare reforms. A defeat had been predicted by the polls but not quite on that scale.The roles are reversed this time, with the Democrats in opposition and the economy on the minds of voters. But there are a number of reasons why Democrats may not have as good a night as history might suggest or as some might expect, given Trump's low approval rating.Firstly, much of the territory in play in this election Trump conquered with ease in the presidential election just two years ago. It's like a home game for Republicans.Then there have been changes to House election boundaries over the years that have meant fewer seats switch between parties.Thirdly, there are fewer swing voters due to the deeper polarisation of the country. Some experts describe the electorate as calcified.There's also the cash advantage Republicans have enjoyed which has given them hundreds of millions of dollars to spend on attack ads in the final weeks.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Obama gives a press conference the day after the heavy 2010 midterms defeatPolling models try to capture shifting fundamentals. And a well-designed poll is built to anticipate issues that may make it less than reliable.Individual polls do have a built-in margin of error – a statistical level of uncertainty based on the sampling size compared to the population as a whole. Taken as an aggregate, polling averages and not individual surveys can provide a more accurate prediction.At the moment, even the kind of polling lean we saw in recent presidential elections would suggest Democrats are likely to have a good night on 3 November. And polling inaccuracies can go both ways. In last year's state and special elections, Democrats outperformed most surveys as it was their voters who turned out in unexpectedly larger numbers.The sight of Trump holding rallies in the final days of the campaign in states he won comfortably in 2024 will have lifted Democrats' hopes that Republican internal polling has conservative candidates in trouble.Figure caption, Voter voices: What issues matter most to Americans?There's always the chance that voters change their minds right up until election day, however.Sometimes there are late shifts that can alter the dynamics of a race. Sometimes undecided voters, which still account for a key segment of the electorate in many of these races, all break the same way.In polling, there will always be some level of uncertainty – and managing that is the art that goes along with the science."I think we're doing a better job," says Young. "But part of the problem we always have is not just with the pollsters. Part of it is that we're dealing with humans. Humans are not easy."Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Democrats have high hopes for midterms, but polls have let them down before
